instructor: While I have great respect for Aykut Hoca as an individual, I must say that as an instructor, he faces challenges in providing helpful and engaging classes to students with diverse backgrounds who are involved in various research fields. The course was 40% about entropy and 80% about DNA.  Aykut Hoca has no tolerance for our different backgrounds. A student with a background in engineering or physics would have significant difficulties during this course. Leave the classes alone, I dedicated a significant amount of time to studying for the quizzes, just to see biology-related questions that indirectly assume prior knowledge of biology, which is unfair. The quizzes include questions on the lecture notes of a previously invited guest speaker, which is nonsensical.The midterm was a disaster. He assured us that he is not grade-oriented and that we would receive  points if we attempted the solution. However, I got zero on a question in which I attempted a solution but did not arrive at the precise answer. In addition, there were several questions that might have had multiple valid answers because they were unclear and not correctly stated, however, he only accepted one answer. The TA is also so strict while grading the quizzes. During the midterm, he arrived 20 minutes late and initially refused to give additional time until we mentioned it. The worst problem in the midterm was a question that required the use of the autocorrelation formula, which he had never taught us. This formula is not something that can be derived easily; it is rather lengthy. Still, he expected us to be familiar with it. The midterm was completely nonsensical. Although not particularly hard, the course is tailored for biology students. The syllabus should be revised and customized to students with different backgrounds. The quizzes should be simpler and centered on the slides covered in class and the midterm, ideally, should cover topics related to materials science and nanotechnology students.

The strongest aspect was that the professor conducted the class in a friendly manner. It was suitable for students with background from any discipline, be it biological or physical sciences. His quiz questions, homework questions and even some of the exam questions were also open ended. This was fun since such questions help student to be in research mood whenever answering questions. For this reason, even if two students have different answers, they both got 100 as long as there is proper justification.

However, there were some weak aspect of this instructor such as not proctoring the exams. During the midterm exam, he left students alone for sometime and some of the students used their smartphone. This same thing happened with quiz 10 and onwards with student who were consistently using their smartphone during quiz. There was no TA or professor in the classroom. After distributing the questions, the TA/instructor used to leave the room for around 10 minutes. These incidents were bad experience for us. In the midterm, there were some problem with question printing, that's why he gave us some extra time and sent us to a different room in the third floor. But there was no TA again and some students were literally discussing with each other and verifying their answer using internet. In the middle of the semester, I almost lost my morale and grew a little hatred towards the course for these reason. I sincerely believe from the next semester, the instructor will take necessary action so that students will not cheat. 

Last thing is about a midterm question where the instructor asked us to solve a question about autocorrelation but he never showed how to solve such question. After the midterm, he showed us how to solve such question. If he showed us the approach before the midterm, it would help us more. Also, there are lots of spelling mistake and some logical mistake in the slides. So overall, he is a good professor but lacks some qualities to be very good. 6.5/10

Dr. Aykut Erbaş stands out as a highly effective educator who succeeds in making the course accessible and understandable, especially for students with a background in biology. Although MSN 518 is one of the most demanding courses in the program due to its intensive content and the combination of assignments, quizzes, midterm, and final exam, the clear and structured way in which Dr. Erbaş presents the material ensures coherence and supports the learning process. I also believe he made a sincere effort to help us succeed in the course.

As a student coming from the life sciences, I found his interest in biological systems and his effort to incorporate them into the course content particularly valuable. Despite being a physicist by training, his willingness to engage with biology and integrate it into his teaching greatly supported interdisciplinary learning. This approach made the course both more engaging and more comprehensible for me. His use of biology-related examples during lectures and his overall attitude that encouraged students to trust their own academic foundations were highly supportive and motivating.

On the other hand, at times I found the workload to be excessive. The overall intensity of the course, combined with frequent quizzes, extensive assignments, and a demanding exam schedule, made time management particularly challenging. A more balanced workload or a slight reduction in content density could allow students to engage more deeply with the material. In particular, Homework 5, which involved setting up a laboratory environment, did not fully align with the course’s main learning objectives and felt overly detailed. A lighter workload or a better integration of biological applications could enhance the learning experience and better reflect the direct relationship between nanotechnology and biology.

Overall, I am satisfied with Dr. Erbaş’s teaching and appreciate his academic approach in bridging disciplines effectively.
course: The strongest aspect of the course is its comprehensive and interdisciplinary content, offering insights into nanoscience from both physics and biology perspectives. For students with a background in life sciences, the integration of biological concepts into a traditionally physics-heavy curriculum made the material more relatable and intellectually engaging. The weakest aspect is the heavy workload. Frequent quizzes, detailed homework assignments, and challenging exams made it difficult to fully absorb the content. While the topics themselves were valuable, the tight deadlines and overall pace sometimes limited deeper reflection. For students coming from a biology background, a more simplified and digestible presentation of physics-based concepts could have further enhanced the learning experience. Additionally, only Raman spectroscopy was covered as a hands-on component, followed by a related quiz. It seems that the instructor has recently started placing more emphasis on characterization methods within the course content. I find this direction very valuable and would suggest expanding such practical components, ideally to include other characterization techniques as well. This would help students reinforce theoretical knowledge through real-world applications and develop a stronger understanding of the tools used in nanoscience.
